Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes): Acute wheezy breathing and progressive shortness of breath for 2 days after cleaning a dusty carpet. Symptoms worse at night and with talking (unable to complete sentences). History of childhood asthma (mostly resolved) and seasonal hay fever (atopy). Prior courses of oral steroids for asthma (past). No other chronic diseases documented.  
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes): Not recorded.  
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines: Has an asthma inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented. Reports prior oral steroids for asthma in the past — dose/route/frequency not documented. No regular medications documented. No antihistamines at home.  
- Immunisation status reviewed (flu, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, tetanus): Not recorded.  
- Sexual/reproductive health status and risks: Not recorded.  
- Lifestyle: physical activity, diet, tobacco, alcohol, substance use: Trigger exposure: house cleaning with dust inhalation. Reports having approximately four to five glasses of water per day. Exercise can provoke symptoms occasionally (reports exercise-induced symptoms when running long distances). No tobacco, alcohol, or other substance use documented.  
- Hearing and vision concerns: Not recorded.  
- Mood, mental health, and risk assessment (depression, anxiety, self-harm): Not recorded.  
- Social context: family support, caregiving, housing, financial stressors: Lives in a house (was cleaning carpet). Able to drive to GP; estimated minutes' drive to surgery. No other social details documented.

- Planned/Recommended investigations from transcript: Attend clinic for finger pulse oximetry (oxygen saturation) and further in-person respiratory assessment; additional respiratory testing at clinic if indicated (not specified).

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key clinical findings and reasoning: Acute onset wheeze and progressive dyspnea beginning ~2 days ago immediately after dust exposure while cleaning. History of childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever indicating atopy. Symptoms worse at night and causing difficulty completing sentences when speaking, suggesting significant airflow limitation. No chest pain, dizziness, syncope, or systemic allergic signs recorded. No objective respiratory measurements recorded in the consultation.  
- Relevant differentials from DDx supporting/refining clinician impression:
  - Asthma exacerbation (allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm) — High likelihood (supported by history of childhood asthma, atopy, temporal relation to dust exposure, nocturnal worsening, speech limitation).  
  - Allergic upper airway reaction / allergic bronchospasm (non-anaphylactic) — Medium likelihood (supported by dust trigger and atopy; lacks systemic anaphylaxis features).  
  - Acute viral bronchitis / reactive airways post-infection — Medium likelihood (possible cause of wheeze but less supported given clear dust trigger and absence of infectious symptoms).  
- Working diagnosis: Asthma exacerbation (allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm). Justification: acute wheeze after dust exposure in a patient with prior asthma and hay fever; consistent with DDx high-likelihood ranking.  
- Considerations (additional plausible but uncertain options from DDx): Allergic bronchospasm (medium), viral bronchitis/reactive airways (medium), inhalational irritant-induced bronchospasm (medium). Pulmonary embolism and anaphylaxis considered but judged less likely by DDx (low likelihood) given context and absent supporting features.  
- Management plan documented in transcript:
  - Immediate: advised to attend an in-person clinic for assessment and pulse oximetry.  
  - Symptomatic: advised that an oral antihistamine may be reasonable if an allergic trigger is suspected; patient does not have one at home and was advised she can purchase OTC or obtain a prescription from GP.  
  - Possible need for oral steroids if assessment indicates significant asthma exacerbation (clinician noted steroids may be needed after clinic assessment).  
  - Administrative: clinician will write and send a letter to the patient's GP summarizing the episode and recommending GP review; patient advised visit to GP likely brief (~10 minutes).  
- Conflict noted: None between transcript and DDx.

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification: Advice to obtain antihistamine if allergic trigger suspected and to seek prompt in-person assessment; no chronic disease prevention counseling documented.  
- Patient health goals and priorities: Not recorded.  
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA): Not recorded.  
- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports): Referral/action: attend GP/clinic for respiratory assessment; clinician to send letter to GP. No other referrals documented.  
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled: Follow-up: advised to present to GP/clinic for assessment; no formal appointment time or recall scheduled in transcript.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Asthma exacerbation (allergic/irritant-triggered bronchospasm) — High. Justification: Acute wheeze after dust exposure in patient with history of childhood asthma and atopy; progressive dyspnea and speech limitation consistent with significant airflow obstruction.  
- Allergic upper airway reaction / allergic bronchospasm (non-anaphylactic) — Medium. Justification: Temporal relationship to dust exposure and atopy support localized allergic bronchospasm; absence of systemic anaphylaxis signs lowers likelihood.  
- Acute viral bronchitis / reactive airways post-infection — Medium. Justification: Viral/reactive airways can cause progressive wheeze in atopic individuals, but lack of infectious symptoms and clear dust trigger make this less favored.

Quality checks

- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vital signs (pulse oximetry, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure), lung auscultation findings, peak expiratory flow or spirometry, medication doses/frequencies, immunisation status, smoking/alcohol history, and basic screening tests (blood tests, ECG) are not recorded.  
- Internal conflicts or contradictions between transcript and DDx: None identified.  
- Transcript quality notes: Brief loss of video signal noted during consultation; audio includes some short pauses and minor repetition but key clinical details (history of exposure, symptoms, past asthma/hay fever, prior steroids, lack of antihistamines) are documented.
